title: Who was Dr. Bronner?
summary: Oft-requested episode about Dr. Bronner's Magic Soap and its founder Emanuel Heilbronner (born Emil Heilbronner, self-styled "Dr." Bronner). Covers his family's Jewish soap-making business in Germany, emigration to New York in 1929, marriage to Paula Voldefought, the Holocaust-era deaths of his parents and siblings, his wife's death, his neglect of his three children, his "Moral ABC" and six cosmic principles printed on the label, the 1945 Chicago publicity crucifixion stunt involving Fred Walker, his 1946 arrest and commitment to Elgin State Hospital and escape to Los Angeles, the company's founding in 1948, the 1960s hippie-driven revival, his 1950s anti-communist and anti-fluoride views, his sons Jim and Ralph and grandson David's running of the company, its employee and political practices, hemp and psychedelics advocacy, and its growth to near $200 million in revenue. The episode closes with a live tour plea for Atlanta and a Mark Spitz label anecdote.
topics: employee pay compression five to one cap

segments.title: Listener requests and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce an oft-requested episode on Dr. Bronner's after several listeners asked about it, and note the soap's label text and long-running history.

segments.title: Emil Heilbronner's family and early life
segments.summary: The Heilbronner family made soap in Germany from 1858. Emil trained as an apprentice in castile soap making, was estranged from his family over Zionism, and emigrated to New York in December 1929 at age 21 just after the stock market crash.

segments.title: Marriage, first soap product, and name change
segments.summary: Emil married German immigrant Paula Voldefought in 1930 and made a peppermint oil soap in 1935 that later became the top seller. He became a naturalized citizen in 1936 and changed his name to Emanuel Theodore Bronner, self-bestowing the title of doctor.

segments.title: Nazi persecution and family losses
segments.summary: The Nazis forced the family's soap business to be sold, and Jewish citizens were barred from taking capital out of Germany. His parents and siblings were sent to concentration camps and killed. A final postcard from his father reportedly said 'you were right'.

segments.title: Wife's death and his absent parenting
segments.summary: His wife became depressed after a fall and died in a state mental hospital outside Chicago, leaving him a widower with three children. He was largely absent and the children were placed in orphanages and with other families.

segments.title: Moral ABC and the postwar vision
segments.summary: After World War Two Bronner developed a vision that humanity needed to unite as one people, the United States of the world. His sister Louise traced the change in him to the deaths of his parents and wife.

segments.title: Using the soap label to spread the message
segments.summary: The Moral ABC was a continuing work in progress for Bronner's whole life. He realized the soap could carry the message on its label.

segments.title: Chicago years and the 1945 crucifixion stunt
segments.summary: In Chicago Bronner became a street preacher and drew follower Fred Walker, an Austrian immigrant with a movement called American Industrial Democracy. Walker was crucified outside a Chicago train station in March 1945 as a publicity stunt; police questioned Bronner, who handed out peace pamphlets. The University of Chicago's International Center declined his lecture offer.

segments.title: 1946 arrest, Elgin commitment, escape, and Los Angeles
segments.summary: Bronner was arrested in March 1946 and committed to Elgin State Insane Asylum at his sister's request. He described abuse there, which the hosts note is unverified. He escaped three times, finally walking away during a lunch visit with his sister, and made his way to Los Angeles. The company was founded in 1948, and he preached and sold soap at Pershing Square, which led to putting the message on the label.

segments.title: Anti-communist and anti-fluoride campaigns and the 1960s hippie revival
segments.summary: In the 1950s Bronner called the FBI daily about communists and developed a file. He promoted the idea that fluoride was a poisoning plot. In the 1960s IRS trouble over nonprofit registration led him to stop selling soap, until hippies ordered fifty-gallon drums and revived the business.

segments.title: Bronner's personality and business troubles
segments.summary: Bronner loved to talk and took calls on his home phone line in Escondido, California, where the house was also the factory. He was a poor business operator, owed large back taxes, and nearly bankrupted the company by the 1980s. His eldest son Jim turned it around and shaped the Moral ABC into clearer principles.

segments.title: Six cosmic principles and employee benefits
segments.summary: The family distilled the Moral ABC into six cosmic principles covering themselves, customers, employees, suppliers, the earth, and community. The company offered full health coverage with zero deductible, profit sharing, and a five-to-one compensation cap.

segments.title: Political giving, fair trade, and hemp advocacy
segments.summary: The company donated about nine million dollars in 2022, roughly a third of net profits, to over 300 nonprofits and publishes an election guide. Grandson David Bronner pushed for legal industrial hemp, was arrested in 2009 for planting hemp outside DEA headquarters, and the company celebrated hemp legalization in 2018.

segments.title: Psychedelics advocacy and company growth
segments.summary: David Bronner advocates for legalizing psychedelics, and the company's health plan subsidizes ketamine-assisted therapy. Jim and his father both died in the late 1990s, and sales grew strongly in the 2010s and during COVID, nearing $200 million.

segments.title: Product range and Castile soap uses
segments.summary: The company also sells chocolate toothpaste. The hosts discuss the castile soap's many uses listed on the label, and mention a homemade castile soap company from a host's family.

segments.title: Mark Spitz label lawsuit
segments.summary: The hosts recall that Mark Spitz, along with Jesus, Thomas Szasz, and L. L. Zamenhof, appeared on the label. Spitz sued in 2008 and the matter settled for an undisclosed amount.

segments.title: Listener mail and tour plea
segments.summary: The hosts ask Atlanta listeners to attend their live show at Atlanta Symphony Hall on September 7, with other tour dates mentioned, and give contact details.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close with the show credit and iHeartRadio promotion.
